extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Aristotelian philosophy / ethics (scholars, philosophy students)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and explicating Aristotle's classification and definitions of the intellectual faculties (Art, Knowledge, Practical Wisdom, Science, Intuition) and related practical-moral concepts (Good Counsel, Judiciousness, Cleverness, natural vs. matured virtue).

rubrics_metrics.name: List of intellectual faculties (five)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let those faculties whereby the Soul attains truth in Affirmation or Negation be five: viz. Art, Knowledge, Practical Wisdom, Science, Intuition (Supposition and Opinion excluded because by these one may go wrong).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the primary taxonomy: the intellectual parts of the soul that produce truth. Use this five-way division as the basis for distinguishing types of intellectual excellence and their proper objects and operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge (episteme)
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge is 'a state or mental faculty apt to demonstrate syllogistically' — that which strictly and properly speaking we know, cannot be otherwise than it is; its objects are necessary/eternal and it is capable of being taught.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge concerns necessary truths; it is produced by demonstrative reasoning (syllogism) from first principles. Teaching and learning presuppose prior knowledge. Knowledge's premisses must be better known than the conclusion; otherwise the result is merely accidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art (techne)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is 'a certain state of mind, conjoined with true Reason, apt to Make.' It has to do with production, contrivance, and the origination of things which may either be or not be, i.e. contingent things whose origin rests with the maker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art concerns making (production) not doing (action). It handles contingent matters that can be produced; neither necessary nor naturally self-originating things fall under Art. Example: architecture as an Art. Art and Fortune can concern the same kinds of contingent things. The absence of Art is the same state conjoined with false Reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Wisdom (phronesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical Wisdom is 'a state conjoined with reason, true, having human good for its object, and apt to Do.' It is the capacity to deliberate well about what is good and expedient for living well; it operates on contingent matters and is directed to action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinct from Knowledge and Art because it deals with doing rather than making and with contingent ends. Practical Wisdom requires both general principles and knowledge of particulars (details from experience); it aims at right ends, right means, and right timing. It admits of 'supreme' (legislation) and 'subordinate' (politike: action and deliberation) forms. One cannot be Practically-Wise without moral goodness; Practical Wisdom does not admit degrees in the same way Art does.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science (scientific knowledge / episteme)
rubrics_metrics.description: Science denotes the most accurate form of Knowledge — the union of Knowledge and Intuition; the Scientific man possesses truth respecting First Principles and is the most accurate of all Knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science is applied both to excellence of art (a 'scientific' sculptor) and to highest theoretical knowledge (possession of first principles). Science's objects are the most precious and immutable things; it cannot be identical with practical wisdom because its objects and aims differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intuition (nous)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intuition is the faculty that takes in First Principles — the apprehension of indemonstrable, first truths which cannot be proved syllogistically and which underpin demonstrative reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuition is neither Knowledge nor Art nor Practical Wisdom; it supplies the indemonstrable premises for demonstration. Intuition comes in practical and theoretical forms: it grasps immutable first terms for demonstrative reasoning and the contingent 'extremes' (particulars) for practical matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for demonstrative knowledge (requirements of premises)
rubrics_metrics.description: For demonstrative reasoning to produce Knowledge, premises must be true, first (indemonstrable), incapable of syllogistic proof, better known, prior in order of time, and causes of the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A demonstration (syllogism that produces Knowledge) requires premisses that are prior and better known than the conclusion and that are causal. Principles that are necessary to learn something else are axioms; a thesis (θέσις) is indemonstrable and unnecessary for learning something else. The knower must believe the contradictories of principles firmly (infallibility ideal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Good Counsel (right deliberation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good Counsel is 'Rightness in respect of what conduces to a given End,' i.e. rightness of deliberation apt to attain good; it is not Knowledge, Opinion, Happy Conjecture, nor mere quick perception of causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good Counsel involves enquiry and calculation (deliberation) and requires proper ends, means, and timing. It must aim at what is expedient and attain the end by right means (not merely accidentally). It can be general or directed toward a particular end. Good Counsel is a quality of those with Practical Wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between deliberation and enquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberation is a kind of enquiring but differs from mere enquiry; deliberating is enquiring and calculating about what to do, whereas enquiry may be broader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberation is temporally longer (deliberate slowly, execute quickly) and aims at action; hence faculties involved differ from those of quick conjecture or mere opinion. Right deliberation is necessary for Good Counsel and Practical Wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judiciousness / γνώμη (right judgment, equity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The faculty called γνώμη (judiciousness) is 'the right judgment of the equitable man' — the capacity to make allowance and equitable decisions; it is neither identical with Knowledge nor a special science but shares the object-matter of Practical Wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judiciousness is the use of the opinionative faculty to judge well concerning matters that fall under Practical Wisdom when another enunciates them; it is the disposition to make allowance and to reach equitable judgments. It is not identical with possessing Practical Wisdom or with attaining it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleverness (ability to adapt means to ends)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a faculty (commonly named Cleverness) that enables one to do and attain whatever conduces to any given purpose; if the purpose is good the faculty is praiseworthy, if not it denotes mere ability to do anything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cleverness is distinct from Practical Wisdom: it adapts means to ends but does not guarantee the rightness of ends. Practical Wisdom includes this adaptive power but only when joined with moral goodness; Vice distorts moral vision and thus distorts practical syllogisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural Virtue vs. Matured (acquired) Virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish Natural Virtue (dispositions present by nature in children and brutes) from Matured Virtue (virtue in the highest sense). Natural dispositions (justice, self-mastery, courage) require an intellectual element to become true virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matured Virtue cannot be formed without Practical Wisdom (the intellectual element). The analogy: Natural Virtue to Matured Virtue is as Cleverness to Practical Wisdom. Matured Virtues together constitute the state of being 'good' in the highest sense and require the unity provided by Practical Wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience, particulars, and age for Practical Wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical Wisdom requires knowledge of particulars and details (particular facts) which are gained from experience and length of time; hence the young may be scientific or mathematical but not possessed of Practical Wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because practical judgement depends on particulars that come from experience, Practical Wisdom often requires age and lived experience. Mathematics is acquired via abstraction, whereas principles of natural philosophy and practical particulars are gained by experiment and experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees and moral evaluation differences between Art and Practical Wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: Art admits of degrees of excellence and one who errs purposely in Art may be preferable to one who errs unwittingly; Practical Wisdom and the moral virtues do not admit this kind of ranking — wrongdoing purposely is worse for moral virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use different evaluative standards when assessing excellence in making (Art) versus moral action (Practical Wisdom/virtues). In Art, deliberate error with knowledge may be better than ignorant error; in moral virtues, deliberate vice is not preferable.
